messages.body_plain:
I guess it should be possible to create a new geom for this, although
I'm not quite convinced how well it represents the data (but then
again, I don't fully understand regular boxplots...)

A starting point would be to create a grob like this,

library(grid)
#' bloated box plot
#'
#' @aliases bboxGrob grid.bbox
#' @title bboxGrob
#' @param x coordinates
#' @param y coordinates
#' @return a grob
#' @seealso \code{grid.segments}, \code{grid.points}
#' @examples
#' r <-
#' gboxplot()
#' pushViewport(viewport())
#' grid.draw(r)

library(grid)
gboxplot <- function( x =seq(0, 1, len=100), y = rnorm(100, 0.6, 0.02),
                     ymin=0.2, lower=0.4, middle=0.7,
                     upper=0.8, ymax=0.9,
                     width=0.5) {
# smoothed data
 b <- gList(
            rectGrob(x = unit(0.5, "npc"), y = lower,
         width = unit(width, "npc"), height = upper - lower,
         just = "bottom", hjust = NULL, vjust = NULL,
         default.units = "npc", name = NULL,
         gp=gpar(fill="grey80"), vp = NULL),
            segmentsGrob(x0=0.5-width/2, y0=middle, x1=0.5+width/2, y1=middle,
                         gp=gpar(col="grey50", lex=2)),
            segmentsGrob(x0=rep(0.5, 2), x1=rep(0.5, 2),
                         y0=c(ymin, upper), y1=c(lower, ymax),
                         gp=gpar(lex=4, lineend="butt")))

 s <- pointsGrob(x, y, vp=viewport(clip=TRUE, width=width))

g <- gTree(children=gList(b, s))
 g
}

and once this is polished enough, an interface (mapping) could be made
via a new ggplot2 Geom. I'm not sure how one would specify the two
different statistics though.

Just a thought anyway,

Best,

baptiste

ltys = c("solid", "dashed", "51","15","11","FFAA")

messages.subject: Faceting: can I change panel heights individually?
messages.subject_clean: Faceting: can I change panel heights individually?
messages.body_plain:
I'm trying again since I got no response to the message titled "Scales
and space in faceting".

Is there a way to have individual control for the panel heights in
faceting? I could use such a feature since I get unpredictable
behavior when using scales="free", space="free".

According to the documentation in Chapter 7,
"For facet_grid there is an additional parameter called space, which
takes values "free" or "fixed". When the space can vary freely, each
column (or row) will have width (or height) proportional to the range
of the scale for that column (or row)."

It seems to work as documented when space = "free" and scales =
"fixed" (in this case the same scale is used in all panels) but not
when scales = "free". Take the following example:

da <- data.frame(
     x=rep(1:5, 2),
     y=c(1+(0:4), 1+(0:4)/10),
     z=rep(1:2, each=5))
da

#   x   y z
#1  1 1.0 1
#2  2 2.0 1
#3  3 3.0 1
#4  4 4.0 1
#5  5 5.0 1
#6  1 1.0 2
#7  2 1.1 2
#8  3 1.2 2
#9  4 1.3 2
#10 5 1.4 2

qplot(x, y, data=da, group=z, geom="line") +
#    scale_y_log10() +
     facet_grid(z~., scales="free_y", space="free")

If the facet heights were proportional to their row ranges, the ratio
of the top to bottom facet heights (i.e., z=1 to z=2) would be (5-1)/
(1.4-1) = 4/0.4 = 10. The observed ratio in the resulting plot is
instead a lot smaller than that.

If you uncomment the line with scale_y_log10() the heights ratio would
be log10(5)/log10(1.4) (since log10(1) = 0), i.e., 4.78. In reality,
the two panel heights look the same in my display!

I'm using R 2.9.1 and ggplot2 0.8.3.

Roberto

messages.subject: How to set default geom with custom stat?
messages.subject_clean: How to set default geom with custom stat?
messages.body_plain:
I've written a stat for the cumulative distribution of x, whose
purpose is similar to the histogram geom. The code is patterned after
StatBin in the ggplot2 source code.

In the simplest case I'd like to do
> qplot(x,data=df,stat="cumdist")
and automatically use geom_step and y = (proportion of observations <=
x).

The stat is mostly working, but I would appreciate help on the
following:

For this plot:
    qplot(x,..p..,data=df,stat="cumdist")
the default geom_point is used even though I included
  default_geom <- function(.) GeomStep
in the definition of StatCumdist.
On the other hand, if I don't specify y, the
  default_aes <- function(.) aes(x=..x..,y = ..p..)
works as intended, but the geom appears as vertical lines from each
(..x.., 0) to (..x.., ..p..). Manually specifying e.g. geom="step" or
geom=c("step","point") works fine. How should I specify the default
geom?

How can I specify default y axis limits to c(0,1)?

Can I have a compound default_geom, like c("step","point")? And could
I make that conditional on the number of points in x, using GeomStep
if there are lots of points?

Thank you in advance for any help!

Best regards,
Jon Olav

StatCumdist <- proto(Stat, {
  objname <- "cumdist"
  desc <- "Cumulative distribution"
  desc_outputs <- list(
    x = "sorted data values",
    n = "number of points <= x",
    p = "proportion of points <= x"
  )
  required_aes <- c("x")

  default_geom <- function(.) GeomStep
  default_aes <- function(.) aes(x=..x..,y = ..p..)

  calculate <- function(., data, scales, ...) {
    x <- sort(data$x)
    n <- seq(along=x)
    p <- n / length(x)
    return(data.frame(x=x, n=n, p=p))
  }

  examples <- function(.) {
    df <- data.frame(x=runif(10),a=(runif(10)>0.3))
    qplot(x,..p..,data=df,stat="cumdist")
    qplot(x,..p..,data=df,stat="cumdist",geom=c("step","point"))
    # I would like to shorten this to
    # qplot(x,data=df,stat="cumdist")
  }

})

stat_cumdist <- StatCumdist$build_accessor()
StatCumdist$examples()

messages.body_plain:
Hi -

    I'm finally moving from the base graphics to ggplot2, but have
encountered some difficulty in migrating multiple plot (and multiple
page) layouts on a pdf device. Using the base package, this is as easy
as the following (repeated for each page and assumes the pdf() device
is active):

x<-1:10; y<-rnorm(x); # Dummy data
old.par <- par(no.readonly = TRUE); # Store par()
par(mfrow=c(2,3),oma=1*c(1,1,1,1)); # Set layout for a single page

messages.subject_clean: ggplot2/ grid equivalents for mfrow and mtext
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I've just tried to improve a little helper function for this purpose (*),

arrange <- function(..., nrow=NULL, ncol=NULL, as.table=FALSE,
main=NULL, sub=NULL, plot=TRUE) {
	dots <- list(...)
	n <- length(dots)
	if(is.null(nrow) & is.null(ncol)) { nrow = floor(n/2) ; ncol = ceiling(n/nrow)}
	if(is.null(nrow)) { nrow = ceiling(n/ncol)}
	if(is.null(ncol)) { ncol = ceiling(n/nrow)}
        ## NOTE see n2mfrow in grDevices for possible alternative

fg <- frameGrob(layout=grid.layout(nrow,ncol))

	ii.p <- 1
	for(ii.row in seq(1, nrow)){
	ii.table.row <- ii.row
	if(as.table) {ii.table.row <- nrow - ii.table.row + 1}
		for(ii.col in seq(1, ncol)){
			ii.table <- ii.p
			if(ii.p > n) break
	        	fg <- placeGrob(fg, ggplotGrob(dots[[ii.table]]),
row=ii.table.row, col=ii.col)
			ii.p <- ii.p + 1
		}
    }

        if(!is.null(main) | !is.null(sub)){
            g <- frameGrob() # large frame to place title(s) and content
            g <- packGrob(g, fg)
            if (!is.null(main))
                g <- packGrob(g, textGrob(main), side="top")
            if (!is.null(sub))
                g <- packGrob(g, textGrob(sub), side="bottom")
        } else {
            g <- fg
        }

        if(plot) grid.draw(g)
        invisible(g)
}

library(ggplot2)
plots = llply(1:5, function(.x) qplot(1:10,rnorm(10),main=paste("plot",.x)))

arrange(plots[[1]],plots[[2]],plots[[3]], nrow=2, as.table=TRUE,
main="test main", sub="subtitle test")

A few improvements that I'd like to make in the future:

- ideally one could mix 'regular' grobs and ggplot2 objects, but I'm
not sure how to deal with a input list of mixed classes

- it is painfully slow, probably because of the use of ggplotGrob()
and grid.pack (the latter could be easily circumvented)

- I guess one would want some options regarding the formatting of the
main and sub titles

ideas are welcome

HTH,

baptiste

(*) this code will eventually appear in the gridextra package at
http://code.google.com/p/gridextra/

messages.body_plain:
See below for constructive criticism of each plot. Overall, it's done
very well and it's a very fun idea to let Ss play with their data
afterwards like this.

Religious Beliefs
- I wouldn't use bars in the beliefs plot. I pretty much never use
bars personally, and they certainly don't make sense on a scale with
no true zero (i.e. you arbitrarily set disbelieve as zero).
- Add an error bar to the aggregate data (i.e. not the particular
participant's response). A 95% confidence interval would be nice, or maybe
Fisher's LSD (plot half the LSD on each side of the mean).
- Remove the "Average\nresponse\n" from key labels in all sub plots
(eg. split by gender). In fact, the redundant mapping between the
x-axis and color could be considered chart junk, so maybe the key can
be dropped completely. Keep the color if you really want, but
certainly drop the key.
- You have pretty long x-axis labels; why not maintain the theme from
the demographic data and put the class variables on the y-axis and
data on the x-axis?

Association between religious beliefs and need satisfaction
- this graph does indeed require a key, but remove the
"Average\nresponse\n" from key labels in all sub plots (eg. split by
gender).

Mood and self-esteem scores
- all the notes from Religious Beliefs apply here.

-Mike

On Fri, Sep 4, 2009 at 9:54 AM, Ista Zahn<ista...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Thanks for your suggestions Mike, all good points. A few follow-up
> questions/comments (in-line below):
>
> On Thu, Sep 3, 2009 at 7:06 PM, Mike Lawrence<Mike.L...@dal.ca> wrote:
>> - Add an error bar to the aggregate data (i.e. not the particular
>> participant's response). A 95% confidence interval would be nice, or maybe
>> Fisher's LSD (plot half the LSD on each side of the mean).
>
> Agreed. The question is, what kind of geom to use? I'm thinking the
> pointrange geom might be best, with the lines representing 95%
> confidence intervals. Does that sound reasonable?

I'm a geom_point + geom_errorbar man myself, but geom_point +
geom_pointrange is reasonable too.

>> - Remove the "Average\nresponse\n" from key labels in all sub plots
>> (eg. split by gender). In fact, the redundant mapping between the
>> x-axis and color could be considered chart junk, so maybe the key can
>> be dropped completely. Keep the color if you really want, but
>> certainly drop the key.
>
> The issue I have with this is that the x-axis is not visible without
> scrolling down the page, while the key is visible much sooner. I
> recognize that it is redundant but I really don't want to make people
> scroll all the way down just to figure out what the graph is telling
> them. Thoughts?

While it's "work" for the reader to have to look to the bottom of the
plot for info on that axis, it's work that the reader expects to have
to do. On the other hand, when presented with redundant info in a key,
they don't know it's redundant until they see the axis and can
potentially become confused (like I was for a bit). Maybe a smart
reader will see all unique values from the key demarcated by unique
bins on the x axis in each plot and deduce the redundancy, but I
wouldn't want to rely on that.

>> - You have pretty long x-axis labels; why not maintain the theme from
>> the demographic data and put the class variables on the y-axis and
>> data on the x-axis?
>>
> I considered this, but I feel like it's breaking a convention that
> many people are used to (or maybe just me...). Personally I find it a
> lot harder to compare values when graphs are presented this way.

I grant that the user's previous experience with conventions should be
taken into account when designing a graphic, but I'd argue that
sometimes conventions can arbitrarily narrow design in ways that
hinder effective communication of information. These cases are always
hard to quantify, but I'd argue that long axis labels is a good case
for placing the independent variable on the y-axis for easy reading.
An example is my entry to the case study competition:
http://ggplot2.wik.is/Case_study_competition/Case_study_entry%3a_Reliability_of_and_correlations_between_attention_networks

Cheers,

Mike

Hi Ista,
Looked at your site, the site design is nice. Have you thought about the
scalability of your graphs?
As more people take the survey, some of the plots will become very
dense. You may want to start
now plotting bivariate densities, or at least play with random data that
is the size you expect over time.
Also in the demographic summaries, I would include a dot with the
annotation.

On a more statistical note, have you thought about more aggregate
measures for your survey? Factor analysis?
It seems that there will be some latent variables. Also, web surveys, as
I am sure you are aware are inherently biased
do you have any thoughts about augmenting with data collected from other
modalities?

Nicholas

This is a limitation of qplot - it always uses the point geom, unless
you override it in the call.  Getting the code write so it works
correctly with user specified geoms and/or stats is very tricky.  I'd
recommend creating a geom alias.

There's not really anyway to do this, but you can cheat and in

Not at a high level.  See GeomSmooth for an example of combining two

messages.body_plain:
library(ggplot2)

Whenever the built in ggplot2 summaries can't do what you want, it's
usually best to start doing it yourself.  You can compute the per
model displacement means as follows:

means <- ddply(mpg, c("manufacturer", "model"), summarise,
 displ = mean(displ))

You can then add it to your plot as follows:

qplot(displ, reorder(model, displ), data = mpg) +

  geom_point(data = means, colour = "red", size = 2) +
  facet_grid(manufacturer~., space="free", scales="free_y")

Regards,

Hadley

messages.subject: Bug in geom_hline() with scale_y_log10()
messages.subject_clean: Bug in geom_hline() with scale_y_log10()
messages.body_plain:
It seems that, when used together with scale_y_log10(), geom_hline()
requires as y intercept the log10 of the y intercept, instead of the y
intercept itself. I don't think this is the desired behavior. It's
certainly not the way that abline(h=...) behaves with plot( ... ,
log="y").

For instance,

da <- data.frame(x=1:2, y=c(1, 10))
qplot(x, y, data=da) +
    scale_y_log10() +
    geom_hline(yintercept=1, colour="red")

The red line is drawn at y=10 instead of y=1.

Thanks, Hadley, for looking at this and for the reply to my previous
post on faceting scales.

Roberto

messages.subject: Lattice layout behavior for facet_wrap
messages.subject_clean: Lattice layout behavior for facet_wrap
messages.body_plain:
When you supply Lattice's "layout" argument with a row, column vector
whose product will result in panel layout that's smaller than the
number of panels the factors you're conditioning on will generate,
Lattice will render n pages of that layout for you.   For example, if
I the conditioning I give would generate 48 panels, but I supply the
layout a vector c(4,4), lattice will generate 3 screens in
succession.   Is there anyway to get facet_wrap to behave in a similar
manner?

Thanks,

Paul

messages.subject: References supporting the default aspect of ggplot2 graphics
messages.subject_clean: References supporting the default aspect of ggplot2 graphics
messages.body_plain:
Hello everyone,

I just received back a manuscript in which I used ggplot2 exclusively
for the graphics (and it was kind of accepted, yay!). I tried to
follow the guidelines of the journal (fonts, dimensions, no color,
etc.) while retaining some of what make ggplot2 look and work great
(grey background, grid lines, legends outside the plotting panel,
etc.). In the edited copy, the editorial office basically recommends
that I remove all that. The book underlines that the default choices
of ggplot2 are there for a reason and, while I will conform to the
request of the editorial office, I would also like to point why the
plots where formated that way in the first place. My secret hope is
that the person in the editorial office who proofread the manuscript
was just part of the technical staff and applied the recommendations
without giving them any thoughts. Maybe someone higher up (the
editor?) could take the decision to accept the look of ggplot graphics
if it is correctly justified.

So here is my question: could someone (Hadley?) please point me
towards academic references that justify the defaults for ggplots (in
particular the grey background, the grid lines and the formatting of
legends)? I saw the references to the books by Tufte (1990, 1997,
2001, 2006) in the ggplot book, but I am looking for something more
precise (or at least some page ranges in those books since I don't
have access to any of these in my current position). And having
several authors concur on the subject would help because, even though
Tufte is considered the reference in this domain, the editor of the
journal I am writing for is not likely to know his work and could see
this as just one man's opinion.

Thanks very much in advance,

JiHO
---
http://maururu.net

A start (on gridlines) comes from a previous post by Hadley (thread:
http://groups.google.com/group/ggplot2/browse_thread/thread/c0e47f343e119f7):

~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
From: hadley wickham <h.wick...@gmail.com>
Date: Thu, 2 Jul 2009 09:06:12 -0500
Local: Thurs, Jul 2 2009 11:06 am
Subject: Re: Getting rid of horizontal grid lines
On Fri, Jun 26, 2009 at 12:41 PM, Peter

Flom<peterflomconsult...@mindspring.com> wrote:
> The whole question gets interesting.
> How much of the lines are what Tufte would call 'chartjunk'?  I am sure Tufte would
> prefer that graphs contain a lot fewer gridlines than most ggplot graphs contain.  I am
> also sure that I think Tufte goes too far .... his aesthetic purity of "bits of info per square inch"
> sacrifices some clarity.  It's not how much info you can cram onto a page, it's how much the reader
> can get out, and how easily.

I agree.  See the following paper for an example of why you shouldn't
accept Tufte's advice uncritically:

W. A. Stock and J. T. Behrens. Box, line, and midgap plots: Effects of
display characteristics on the accuracy and bias of estimates of
whisker length. Journal of Educational Statistics, 16(1): 1–20, 1991.

And section 3 of the following paper gives some concrete reasons why
you actually want grid lines:

W. Cleveland. A model for studying display methods of statistical
graphics. Journal of Computational and Graphical Statistics, 2:
323–364, 1993. URL http://stat.bell-labs.com/doc/93.4.ps.

~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

On Sep 3, 3:53 pm, baptiste auguie <bapt4...@googlemail.com> wrote:
> - it is painfully slow, probably because of the use of ggplotGrob()
> and grid.pack (the latter could be easily circumvented)

I have looked into this a bit today, and think much of the time
results from the re-rendering of each plot instead of placing
everything into a gTree then rendering.

The following call stack appears to trigger the initial render
(ConvertX() onward lie in the grid package environment):
ggplotGrob() -> panelGrob() -> <proto>$facet$add_guides() -> max2 ->
to_cm -> ConvertX -> ConvertUnit -> grid.Call -> .Call(L_gridDirty)

I would suggest amending the ggplotGrob() function (or more
specifically, the "max2"/"to_cm" function -- as well as any other
similar functions) to permit the creation of a gTree object without
any rendering so that users may quickly aggregate multiple ggplots
(though I suspect this is the intent of the ggplot::grid* functions
currently under development??). I am uncertain as to whether or not
the grid package really needs to activate a display device to perform
the unit conversion.

HTH

Will

messages.subject: Re: Lattice layout behavior for facet_wrap
messages.subject_clean: Lattice layout behavior for facet_wrap
messages.body_plain:
On Sep 5, 2:00 am, paulie p <pjpug...@earthlink.net> wrote:
> When you supply Lattice's "layout" argument with a row, column vector
> whose product will result in panel layout that's smaller than the
> number of panels the factors you're conditioning on will generate,
> Lattice will render n pages of that layout for you.   For example, if
> I the conditioning I give would generate 48 panels, but I supply the
> layout a vector c(4,4), lattice will generate 3 screens in
> succession.   Is there anyway to get facet_wrap to behave in a similar
> manner?

I don't know of a short way to do this, but here is a poor man's
solution based on "for", %+% and subset():

# Turning on plot history:
windows(record = TRUE)

# A plot facetting on clarity only:
p <- qplot(carat, ..density.., data = diamonds,
   geom = "histogram", binwidth = 0.2) + facet_wrap(~clarity)

# Print the plot, subsetting data to each level of `cut` in turn:
for (i in levels(diamonds$cut)) {
    print(p %+% subset(diamonds, cut == i))
}

(The %+% operator specifies a new data frame for the plot.)

This is limited to putting each level of `clarity` on a separate page,
and assumes that `cut` is a factor. For a string or integer you could
use:
for (i in unique(diamonds$cut))
To convert a continuous variable to a factor, see ?cut and ?
lattice::equal.count.

Hope this helps,
Jon Olav

Oh, I finally get it - sorry for being so dense.  Basically what you
want is 90 degree rotation of geom_line - you can get that with
coord_flip, but coordinate systems do not currently interact well with
free scales.  An alternative is to use geom_path, which connects
points in the in order which they appear in the data:

library(ggplot2)

means <- ddply(mpg, c("manufacturer", "model"), summarise,
 displ = mean(displ))

means <- means[with(means, order(manufacturer, displ)), ]

qplot(displ, reorder(model, displ), data = mpg) +

 geom_path(aes(group = 1), data = means, colour = "red") +

 facet_grid(manufacturer~., space="free", scales="free_y")

Regards,

Hadley

messages.body_plain:
> I would suggest amending the ggplotGrob() function (or more
> specifically, the "max2"/"to_cm" function -- as well as any other
> similar functions) to permit the creation of a gTree object without
> any rendering so that users may quickly aggregate multiple ggplots
> (though I suspect this is the intent of the ggplot::grid* functions
> currently under development??). I am uncertain as to whether or not
> the grid package really needs to activate a display device to perform
> the unit conversion.

That's how ggplotGrob does work (hence the name) - it does no
rendering, just creates a gTree object for later rendering.  As
Baptiste says, I think the active device is needed for some of the
unit conversions that I do.

Some of the slowness is because I'm fighting the usual grid way of
doing things - I don't use gpar, I don't use grid's native coordinates
and I know how big everything on the plot should be (apart from the
panels).  I convert many of the units to cm because my feeling is that
should speed things up - instead of having to perform unit conversions
multiple times, I force grid to do them once (OTOH I'm not sure this
actually helps).

The gridGrob family of functions is my first (slow) attempt to
generalise the layout pattern I'm using.  Any suggestions for making
it faster would be gratefully received.

Hadley

messages.body_plain:
> So here is my question: could someone (Hadley?) please point me
> towards academic references that justify the defaults for ggplots (in
> particular the grey background, the grid lines and the formatting of
> legends)? I saw the references to the books by Tufte (1990, 1997,
> 2001, 2006) in the ggplot book, but I am looking for something more
> precise (or at least some page ranges in those books since I don't
> have access to any of these in my current position). And having
> several authors concur on the subject would help because, even though
> Tufte is considered the reference in this domain, the editor of the
> journal I am writing for is not likely to know his work and could see
> this as just one man's opinion.

There's not a lot, unfortunately.  Dan Carr had a couple of nice
articles in the SCGN newsletter:

D. Carr. Using gray in plots. ASA Statistical Computing and Graphics
Newsletter, 2 (5):11–14, 1994. URL
http://www.galaxy.gmu.edu/~dcarr/lib/v5n2.pdf.

D. Carr and R. Sun. Using layering and perceptual grouping in
statistical graphics. ASA Statistical Computing and Graphics
Newsletter, 10 (1):25–31, 1999.

He also has some good general advice in the following article, but I'm
not sure if he specifically mentions gray backgrounds (although he
does use them a lot)

D. Carr. Graphical displays. In A. H. El-Shaarawi and W. W. Piegorsch,
editors, Encyclopedia of Environmetrics, volume 2, pages 933–960. John
Wiley & Sons, 2002. URL
http://www.galaxy.gmu.edu/~dcarr/lib/EnvironmentalGraphics.pdf.

Hadley

--

messages.body_plain:
Hadley, thanks for thinking about this. The dataframe. can be made to
have four cols:

id prop fct val
1  x     a   0.1
1  y     b   0.3

id is a person, prop is the measurement of the person's w.r.t. the
factor fct. Suppose the cross-product prop X fct yields 6 combinations
(prop can be x or y, fct can be a, b, or c). Then every id (person) is
guaranteed to have been measured w.r.t each of these 6 combinations
exactly once.

In other words, every point (x,y) in the scatterplot is a person being
measured on x and on y w.r.t. to some factor fct, and every person
should have exactly 3 such points because there are 3 factors.

messages.body_plain:
ggplot2 is a nice system, though sometimes a bit of a struggle for
this new R user ;-) I have two questions which the code example
illustrates using ggplot2 sample datasets. For now, qplot seems to
provide all I need without going to ggplot. When layering 2 datasets
on the same plot the legends were initially tangled up, but the
documentation's suggestion of specifying "labels=" and "breaks=" in
"scale_xxx_manual" straightened that out.

Question 1: plot p below has my "rates" legend just as I want it. When
I add the rectangle shading layer from another dataset in plot pb, the
first, "rates" legend.key gets blacked out--though the second, new
legend is perfect. I suspect the legend.key problem is related to
ggplot's combining info from the line & rect geoms for a default
legend.key. Specifying labels= and breaks= cleared up some similar
interference between layers, but how might I keep the black shading
out of the geom="line" legend? I tried changing some legend.key theme
settings, but couldn't figure out anything which worked.

Question 2: the example also illustrates a minor question (which I can
fix mechanically, but I'm curious about). Note that the "party" data
in df. presidential are "Republican" & "Democratic" and the first
rectangle on plot pb is blue, even though I specified colors as "red",
"blue" in that order. I can correct this and get red mapped to
Republican by specifying the colors in reverse order. I haven't found
it mentioned, but suspect this behavior is because ggplot2 maps the
color list to the variable=party elements in "alphabetic or ascii sort
order." Is this correct?

Many thanks to Hadley for providing this great tool!

economicsw <- melt(economics,  measure=c("psavert", "uempmed"),
id="date")

p <- qplot(date, value, data=economicsw, geom="line")
p <- p + aes(colour=variable)  +
  scale_colour_manual(name="rates", c("black",  "chartreuse3"),
  labels=c("personal savings", "unemployment"), breaks=c("psavert",
"uempmed"))
p <- p + opts(title = "economics info")
p <- p + ylab("saving, unemp rates")
print(p)

y_max <- max(c(economics$psavert), max(economics$uempmed))
y_min <- min(c(economics$psavert), max(economics$uempmed))
yrng <- c(y_min, y_max)

presidential$variable <- presidential$party

pb <- p + geom_rect(aes( xmin = start, xmax = end, y = NULL, x = NULL,
 fill = party), ymin = yrng[1], ymax = yrng[2], data=presidential) +
  scale_fill_manual(name="critter", values = alpha(c("red", "blue"),
0.2),
  labels = c("elephant", "donkey") )#, breaks=c("Republican",
"Democratic") )
print(pb)

messages.body_plain:
In the help pages hadley provides the following example showing how to
achieve bar charts with y being means of a variable instead of counts.
The example uses qplot however - and not ggplot. Since i would like to
understand ggplot better I would really like to see how this could be
done in ggplot.

# example using qplot
library(ggplot2)
meanprice <- tapply(diamonds$price, diamonds$cut, mean)
cut <- factor(levels(diamonds$cut), levels = levels(diamonds$cut))
qplot(cut, meanprice, geom="bar", stat="identity", fill = I("grey50"))

messages.subject: Re: bar chart with means - using ggplot
messages.subject_clean: bar chart with means - using ggplot
messages.body_plain:
If you just want to plot the summary data using ggplot then you would do:

ggplot(data.frame(cut, meanprice), aes(cut, meanprice)) +
  geom_bar(stat = "identity", fill = "grey50")

If you want to skip the summarising step then one way would be:

ggplot(diamonds, aes(cut, price)) +
  stat_summary(fun.y = "mean", fill = "grey50", geom = "bar")

But notice the y-axis extends to the range of price.  We can't use
ylim here since it will exclude some of the data which we are
summarising over.  So instead use coord_cartesian:

ggplot(diamonds, aes(cut, price)) +
  stat_summary(fun.y = "mean", fill = "grey50", geom = "bar") +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0,5000))

And maybe add in some more breaks in the axis and change its label:

ggplot(diamonds, aes(cut, price)) +
  stat_summary(fun.y = "mean", fill = "grey50", geom = "bar") +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0,5000)) +
  scale_y_continuous("mean_price", breaks = 1000 * 0:5)

Charlotte

I would recommend not representing means by bars at all.

Bars are for counts, stacking from zero. Means are point estimates.
ggplot has a lot of routines for displaying means with errors bars:
geom_linerange, geom_pointrange. To hone your ggplot skills I
recommend looking into these geoms.

messages.subject: Re: Summary statistic for each facet
messages.subject_clean: Summary statistic for each facet
messages.body_plain:
> Is something similar possible in ggplot2? I know that I can compute
> each facet's correlation outside of ggplot2 and do an annotation with
> geom_text; however it would be more convenient if the calculations
> were done automatically accordingly to the facets specified.

It would be convenient, but to work generally it would require an
infrastructure within ggplot2 for performing any kind of data
manipulation that you can imagine.  I don't think that this is a good
idea in general, so I recommend performing your manipulations outside
of ggplot2.  The plyr package is a natural fit for this sort of
activity:

cors <- ddply(mydf, c("group", "trt"), summarise, cor = cor(x, y))

Hadley

messages.subject_clean: Multiple colours on the same line, with certain differentiating parameters
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I have some normal plot codes to run a graph where certain portions of a particular data series can be highlighted in different colours. I was wondering whether this could be done in ggplot2. This is what I tried:

b<-cumsum(rnorm(1000))
x<-sample(c(1,2), size=1000, replace=TRUE)
y<-sample(c(1,2), size=1000, replace=TRUE)

T<-length(b)
t<-1:(T)

par(mfrow=c(1,2))
plot(t, b, type="n", ax=FALSE, ylab="",xlab="",col=x, ylim=range(b))
title("x")
segments(t,b[t],t+1,b[t+1],col=y)

plot(t, b, type="n", ax=FALSE, ylab="",xlab="",col=x)
title("y")
legend("topleft", legend=c("low","high"), pch=2, col=1:2, merge=FALSE, title="regime", lty=1, bg="white")
segments(t,b[t],t+1,b[t+1],col=x)

library(ggplot2)
tmp <- data.frame(cbind(t,b,x,y))
ggplot(tmp, aes(t))+geom_line(aes(y=b,colour=factor(x)))+labs(x=NULL,y=NULL)

The problem is that I cannot hide those parts of the line that I do not want visible in ggplot, which I could to with the normal plot command.

Am I missing something very obvious?

Regards,
Vimal

messages.subject: Trouble getting stat summary and geom=ribbon to work
messages.subject_clean: Trouble getting stat summary and geom=ribbon to work
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I'm trying to plot a longitudinal data set, using ggplot and adding
some summary info (eg. mean, 1 sd bounds) using geom=ribbon.  The
summary info is based on a subset of the original data (eg. less an
outlier).  But I'm having trouble getting the ribbons to show up
correctly.  It's probably something obvious that I'm missing as a
novice, and any help is much appreciated!

Here's a simple example.  I tried several things.
- if I use geom=crossbar instead of geom=ribbon, everything is ok
- if Day is set as rep(c(1,2,3,8,9), each=8), then everything is ok,
which makes me wonder if the problem has to do with the ordering of
Day?  Day is supposed to be numeric.
- (per Thierry 's suggestion on R help list) calculating summary stats
externally and feeding geom_ribbon the summary stats.  Only Days 1 and
20 came up ok, the other days appeared to be ignored.

Thanks!
Sock

### Example data.  Ran using R version 2.9.2, ggplot2 version 0.8.3
###

set.seed(13)

Day <- rep(c(1, 2, 3, 8, 20), each=8)
# The plot is ok if Day <- rep(c(1,2,3,8,9), each=8)

ID <- rep(LETTERS[1:8], 5)
Y <- rnorm(length(Day), 100, 5)
dat <- data.frame(Day=Day, ID=ID, Y=Y)

 # outlier
dat$Y[dat$ID=="A" & dat$Day==8] <- 150
dat.less <- dat[!(dat$ID=="A" & dat$Day==8),]

# Longitudinal data plot.  Obs for each subject is connected by a line
over time

p <- ggplot(dat, aes(x=Day, y=Y, group=ID)) +
scale_x_continuous(breaks=sort(unique(dat$Day))) +
geom_line(colour=alpha("blue", 5/10))

# Adding mean, 1 sd bounds using crossbar geom is ok.  But the same
info using ribbon geom doesn't work.

p + stat_summary(data=dat.less, aes(group=1), geom="crossbar",
fun.data="mean_sdl", mult=1) + stat_summary(data=dat.less, aes
(group=1), geom="ribbon", fun.data="mean_sdl", mult=1, fill=alpha
("blue", 1/10))

# Calculating summary stats externally and feeding it to geom_ribbon

RibbonData <- ddply(dat.less, "Day", function(x){
        mean(x$Y) + c(ymin = -1, ymax = 1) * sd(x$Y)
})

p + stat_summary(data=dat.less, aes(group=1), geom="crossbar",
fun.data="mean_sdl", mult=1) + geom_ribbon(data = RibbonData, aes
(group= 1, ymin = ymin, ymax = ymax), fill=alpha("blue", 1/10))

This looks like the ordering bug I and several others ran into a while
back. Some numeric data was being sorted alphabetically in some
stat_summary code. It's broken in ggplot2 0.8.3, but fixed in the
development version, fwiw.

http://groups.google.com/group/ggplot2/browse_thread/thread/6e52d349d66c3526/39044af12298774c

Development version: http://github.com/hadley/ggplot2

Installation in some versions of Linux (Windows is trickier):
wget http://github.com/hadley/ggplot2/tarball/master | tar -e
R CMD install hadley-ggplot2-[tab]

 -Harlan

messages.subject_clean: error bars in x- and y-directions?
messages.body_plain:
Dear ggplot2 experts:

I'm still new to this package, but am really thankful that this has
been developed and it's been really fantastic so far! Please keep up
the wonderful work of making beautiful graphs that much easier!

However, I came across an issue where we would like to add error bars
in two directions -- and geom_errorbar works well to show the y-error
bar range as it should.  It probably was wishful thinking after the
documentation said the y-direction only, but I tried something similar
to add an error bar like range in the x-direction to no avail.

Is there possibly some workaround?  I went back to try the
error.crosses in the psych package, but it has not worked on my hands
yet.

qplot(IDPG_mean,IDPG_mean_pet, data = XY_eh) + geom_errorbar(aes
(ymin=IDPG_mean_pet - IDPG_se_pet, ymax=IDPG_mean_pet + IDPG_se_pet))
+ xlab("%ID/g from biodistribution") + ylab("%ID/g from PET") +
geom_errorbar(aes(xmin=IDPG_mean - IDPG_se, xmax=IDPG_mean + IDPG_se))

Many thanks for at least considering this dilemma!
JC

messages.subject: Bug in geom_path when alpha used
messages.subject_clean: Bug in geom_path when alpha used
messages.body_plain:
I found a bug in geom_path when alpha is used. It looks like the alpha
value only works correctly when the colour is set to the same value.
Here's a simple example:

n=10
x=rnorm(n)
y=rnorm(n)
z=seq(n)
w=sample(c("A","B"),10,replace=TRUE)

# This works.
qplot(x,y,colour=z,geom="path",size=I(2))

# This does not (all the line segments have the same alpha value).
qplot(x,y,alpha=z,geom="path",size=I(2))

# This does seem to work, though.
qplot(x,y,alpha=z,colour=z,geom="path",size=I(2))

# And this does not.
qplot(x,y,alpha=z,colour=w,geom="path",size=I(2))

--
Karl Ove Hufthammer

messages.subject_clean: back-to-back bar charts
messages.body_plain:
Hm, poking at this a little... I actually like the two-sided bar
charts as a visualization with the surplus/deficit in the middle.
Here's what I came up with as a first stab:

df <- expand.grid(year=seq(1999,2008),
	type=c("Commodities", "Intermediate", "Final Products",
"Confidential"),
	dir=c("Imports", "Exports"))

df$Value = runif(nrow(df), 5, 30) * ifelse(df$dir=="Imports", -1, 1)

library("ggplot2")

p <- ggplot(df, aes(x=year, y=Value, fill=type)) +
	geom_bar(stat="identity", data=subset(df, dir=="Imports")) +
	geom_bar(stat="identity", data=subset(df, dir=="Exports"))

df.m <- melt(df, id=c("type", "year", "dir"))
df.trade <- cast(df.m, year ~ ., sum)
names(df.trade) <- c("year", "Value")

p <- p + geom_line(data=df.trade, aes(fill=NULL), color="black",
size=2)

The aes(fill=NULL) is required to prevent a decidedly unhelpful eval
error. For reasons I don't yet understand, the line geom crashes if
you don't override the fill=type aesthetic. And there's no legend for
the Trade line. This may be a case where, if you're generating graphs
for publication, some post-hoc editing may be valuable...

Also, the code gives the following warning, despite working fine:

Warning message:
Stacking not well defined when ymin != 0

Anyone know why it would complain in this case?

 -Harlan

Hello,

The newish rms package which is to replace Design says that it works
with ggplot2. However, I have not figured out a quick way to put in
the same sorts of plots with ggplot2.

plot(Predict(fit)) -> plots

ggplot(Predict(fit))
Error: No layers in plot

qplot(Predict(fit))
Error: attempt to apply non-function

ggplot(Predict(cumdsa400.lm), aes(cumdsa400, cumar400),
data=cumdsa400.lm) + geom_point()
Error in ggplot.data.frame(fortify(data), mapping, ...) :
  Mapping should be created with aes or aes_string

Is it that it may work with ggplot, but you have to tell it the
parameters? That doesn't seem to be working either, i.e. telling it
what the x and y should be. I'm sure there is something obvious, but
it is confusing going back and forth between lattice and ggplot
graphics and I've been in lattice mostly of late.

Any suggestions are most appreciated.

Thanks, Aric

Hello, all:

I'm trying to visualize a 2-way contingency table by plotting multiple
lines (line colour = factor levels of variable Y) that show the
proportion of observations (y-axis) at each level of variable X.

Someone in the archives had a similar issue (http://
tolstoy.newcastle.edu.au/R/e5/help/08/10/5907.html <http://tolstoy.newcastle.edu.au/R/e5/help/08/10/5907.html>), but it didn't
quite solve my problem. Here's an example of what I'm trying to do,
using the diamonds dataset:

qplot(cut, ..count../ sum(..count..), colour=color, data=diamonds,
  stat="bin", geom="line", group=color)

However, this plot shows the proportion of observations relative to
the *total* observations [ y = ..count.. / sum(..count..) ]. I want to
plot the proportion of observations to the total obs. *within each
group* -- i.e., the margins of the contingency table rather than the
grand total. I assume this must happen through the 'y' parameter, but
I just can't think of how to do it.

Thanks,
Evan

p.s. - I realize there may be better ways to visualize contingency
tables, like ggfluctuation. I need a line plot, though.

       p <- p + geom_point()
       p <- p + scale_x_continuous("Stated Importances") +

       p <- p + opts(title = paste("Broadview Networks Customer

messages.subject: Re: missing data when axis limits set
messages.subject_clean: missing data when axis limits set
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

This doesn't address the issue.. for me, this is my main complaint
about ggplot, and I'm not sure how to get around it.  It's an issue
with geom_area and geom_line (and presumably _freqpoly), but not R's
native plotting engines.

Here is an example scenario:

 t$x <- seq(100)
 t$y <- dnorm(t$x, mean=50, sd=10)
 ggplot(t) + geom_area(aes(x, y))

That looks like a perfectly normal bell curve.  Now add either ylim
(0,0.02) or scale_y_continuous(limits=c(0,0.02)) into the mix and look
at what you get.  Two spikes with emptiness in the middle.

It's really quite misleading on a number of levels.  Depending on what
the data looks like, your eye may be lead to believe that it's
plotting zero values instead of "off the chart" values.  Even it's
clear that it is not plotting zeroes, it is at the very least
suggesting that you have missing data in those regions... but my input
did not contain any NAs.. there really are plottable values there.

Omitting the out-of-range values (and complaining that you "missed
some data points due to small ylim range") is okay for geom_point, but
not for geom_area or geom_line (especially geom_area).

I suppose the data could be fed through some home-made range-limiting
function before passing it to ggplot, but even that would be somewhat
misleading for, say, situations where we had much less data points.
The slope of the line going off the page would potentially not be
steep enough in some situations.

I am using ggplot2_0.8.2 on R 2.8.1 GUI 1.27 Tiger build 32-bit
(5301).  Perhaps this isn't an issue in other versions or platforms?

Thanks,

messages.subject: Experience with very-large screen projection of ggplot graphics
messages.subject_clean: Experience with very-large screen projection of ggplot graphics
messages.body_plain:
I am producing some graphs that will be part of an upcoming national
conference plenary address (think 7-10K in audience).   So, the graphs
will end up on large  parallel projection screens at a hotel.conference
site, with I suspect medium resolution displays in a badly lit hall.
The graphicss will likely end up "inside" powerpoint for display purposes

Has anyone done this before, and do you have any reflections on font
size, colour choices, etc. that you could offer?  Obviously Tufte's
guidance applies and less is almost always better, and while Hadley has
done a fine job with the defaults, this is a very different graphical
display than paper with high resolution printing. So, experience with
this format of presentation would be most welcome.

Most of the data will be bar charts, box plots, a couple of X/Y graphs,
and some use of geom_crossbar to depict graphically beta estimates and
standard errors from logistic regression models (which, by the way, is a
lovely way to get people to focus on the overall shape of the model
rather than on whether the p value is 0.04 or 0.06).

Suggestions welcome.

Thanks

are high contrast (maybe you'll want theme_bw()), and fill up as much
of the slide as possible - I usually avoid a title, and make the
graphic fill up absolutely every inch of the display.  Another thing
to bear in mind is that with a 10k audience, you'll have ~500 colour
blind men in the audience, so make sure to double check your colours.
I particularly recommend  color oracle
(http://colororacle.cartography.ch/) for this task.

Hadley

messages.subject_clean: Experience with very-large screen projection of ggplot graphics
messages.body_plain:
FWIW, I've noticed that projectors, especially in a darkened room,
typically err on the warm side, ie they cast everything as though
there was a yellow filter over the top.  So while high-contrast will
help there, one additional thing to bare in mind is that yellows will
show even less against the background.

Making the graphics as big as possible is an excellent idea.  I've
effectively zoomed in on sections (and then back out again) when I
want more detail.  I do that as separate slides, without animation,
since animations cause havoc if you have to move backwards in your
presentation (not so likely for a keynote :)  You want to be
particularly careful if you have important parts close to the edge of
your slide, I've found many projectors like to clip small parts of the
edges of slides.  If you are going to zoom, you can do that
effectively with a PDF graphic.

Powerpoint has gotten better about handling imported PDFs, in my quick
testing with PP in Mac Office 2008, PDF came through fine.  I posted a
while back about handling font sizes, best bet is to generate the
picture at the actual size you want, and do no scaling in Word/
Powerpoint.  Use

theme_set(theme_gray(base_size=24)) # or whatever size makes sense for
your slides.
ggsave("test.pdf",width=9,height=7) # 9inx7in is the size that PP
thinks my slides are, according to the rulers.

Note that testing this just now I had some trouble with scales coming
off the edge of the picture at base_size=24.  Seems like the Margins
don't get wider along with the base_size?

--J

messages.subject: Re: missing data when axis limits set
messages.subject_clean: missing data when axis limits set
messages.body_plain:
Right, this is a slightly unintuitive aspect of ggplot. The scale_
(limits=) syntax restricts the *data* (as do its unfortunately named
synonyms xlim and ylim), while the coord_(xlim=) syntax restricts the
*viewport*. Scale_ functions affects the mapping between data and
plot, while coord_ functions just change the plot. In retrospect, some
of these functions and parameters perhaps should have been named
something else...

 -Harlan

On Sep 29, 10:15 am, hadley wickham <h.wick...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > Right, this is a slightly unintuitive aspect of ggplot. The scale_
> > (limits=) syntax restricts the *data* (as do its unfortunately named
> > synonyms xlim and ylim)
>
> But how could the scales work any other way?  If you set
> scale_colour_discrete(limits = c("a", "b")) you don't expect "c" and
> "d" to some how influence the display of the plot, do you?

You don't, and when I think about it, I don't, but people who aren't
experts with ggplot don't yet have a clear understanding of what
"scale" does. Also, it's the first graphing system I've ever used that
lets you restrict the data that way (versus a "subset" type of
command). So, if you're trying to map ggplot's syntax onto your
existing mental models of graphing programs, you're going to assume
that scale_x_continuous(limits=c(1,10)) is going to affect the axis,
not the data. It says "x", and doesn't say "data", so that's a pretty
natural assumption! And the xlim() function is even more likely to be
mapped that way in your head.

>
> > while the coord_(xlim=) syntax restricts the
> > *viewport*. Scale_ functions affects the mapping between data and
> > plot, while coord_ functions just change the plot. In retrospect, some
> > of these functions and parameters perhaps should have been named
> > something else...
>
> Possibly, but unless you come up with completely novel names,
> everything already has some existing meaning to confuse people.

I agree! Not sure what the solution is...

 -Harlan

I'm looking for syntax suggestions, so I don't have a reproducible example. The question is the interaction of stat_summary, facet and geom_boxplot.

I want to generate a horizontally-facetted set of boxplots, with each facet defined by a separate variable,e g. (from diamonds, depth and price)
Within each facet, I'd like to condition the distribution on a categorical variable, e.g. cut.  The simple idea is to be able to compare set of continuous values and look for distributional changes across the categorical variable within each facet.
In my case I want to show that height, weight and bmi across "pre" and "post" periods.  Therefore, it makes sense to have the "pre" and "post" boxplots in the same facet, and then to have the variables change across facets.

So, there must be some incantation of stat_summary or its ilk that will assist with this, but it evades me.

What I am looking for should do something like:

geom_boxplot(aes(x=cut, y=?)+facet_grid(c(depth, price) ~.) where variable is c(depth, price)

but, without having a clear way to specify the  "y" across the two continuous variables depth and price, I'm lost.

Suggestions?

(I recognize that I'll also have to use some sort of scales_free option as well.)

out of curiosity, are there some general guidelines for when a dataset is too big for 'reshape'?

I was fussing with some DNA microarrays in a twin study and wanted to plot correlations within pairs... melt() took about 30 minutes on a box with 64GB of RAM, and cast() took another 20 minutes.

> dim(combined)
[1] 19575   288

If I reduce it to, say, the first 10 principal components then of course it's not so bad.  But that's no good for what I need to do.

I ended up using 'sqldf' and variations on the theme of subset() to manually reshape the data for ggplot2.  Reshape would be an awful lot nicer, though.  I guess I could try parallelizing the lapply() and tapply() calls in melt() and cast(), or swapping in the relevant bits from 'plyr'... ?

What are the guidelines that you have for determining when to use 'melt' and when to do it yourself?  The functions I wrote to rearrange the dataframes runs in a few seconds or less, but it's nowhere near as flexible as using a molten dataset in qplot().  Even if I ran the *apply() loops across 32 worker processes, it seems like melt() and cast() would still be slower than sqldf.

Maybe that's just a reflection of what SQLite is optimized to do -- in which case, maybe there's a way to use SQLite/sqldf instead of 'reshape' for some of these tasks?  Hmmmm.

messages.subject_clean: Can I do this with ggplot2
messages.body_plain:
Hey Gguys/Ggals,

I wanted to start learning how to use ggplot2 and thought I'd try to
redo some functionality found in an existing package (GenomeGraphs)
using ggplot as an exploratory exercise.

The most simple type of pictures that I'm trying to make look like
this:

http://cbio.mskcc.org/~lianos/files/ggplot2/sample.png

* The x axis are positions on the genome.
* I have a 4 vectors that have some real valued number for each
position in the genome, plotted in the Samples1..4 lanes.
* The bottom part (blue boxes) are just the positions of where the
"known" genes are on the same genomic coordinates (see how the real
valued numbers in sample1..4 align pretty well w/ positions of known
gene annotations)

Currently GenomeGraphs is implemented using grid graphics. I'm
wondering if ggplot2 has facilities to control the positions of where
to plot things sufficiently enough to try to attempt a graph like this
using ggplot2 functions.

Just curios if trying this is possible and would be a fruitful
endeavor. Again, I'm not trying to redo the entire package, but simply
trying to get facility with ggplot2 to see what it can do.

Thanks,
-steve

messages.subject_clean: A way to only show every other label on scale_x_discrete?
messages.body_plain:
ggplot2 usually deals pretty well with dates, so why do you use
discrete scales if your values are dates?

To answer your question: you would need to calculate and set the
breaks / labels manually.

Consider the following example, and compare plots p and p1. In the
case of p1, the breaks/labels are set at every third year:
library(ggplot2)

DF <- data.frame(year = as.character(1980:2000), value = 1980:2000)
DF$id <- seq_along(DF$year)

labels <- DF$year[DF$id %% 3 == 1]

p <- ggplot(DF, aes(year, value)) + geom_point()

p1 <- p + scale_x_discrete(breaks = labels, labels = labels)

even.tiny <- function(x) {

}
  }

messages.body_plain:
ggplot2 doesn't support zoo objects, so you need to convert these into
dates either in the data frame or in the ggplot2 aes-call. After that
you can use scale_x_date() to modify minor and major gridlines and
label formatting.

library(zoo)
dat <- zooreg(rnorm(13), start=as.yearmon("2009-01-01"),
frequency=12)

dat1 <- data.frame(index = index(dat), coredata = coredata(dat))

ggplot(dat1) + geom_line(aes(as.Date(index), coredata))

last_plot() + scale_x_date(major="3 months", minor = "3 months",
format="%b-%Y")

--

messages.body_plain:
Okay.  Let me start over.  I had to use as.character() on the year information in order to place the year label directly below the column of data in when using ggplot2 to produce a histogram.

This worked well for small numbers of years of data, but now here is what I am seeing:

Home_SqFootage<-sample(1200:3600, size=sample_size, rep=T)
Home_Year_Built<-sample(1989:2008, size=sample_size, rep=T)
Home_Year_Sold<-sample(1989:2008, size=sample_size, rep=T)

Home_DF<-data.frame(SqFootage=Home_SqFootage, YearBuilt=as.character(Home_Year_Built), YearSold=as.character(Home_Year_Sold))

qplot(YearBuilt, data = Home_DF, binwidth = 1, fill = factor(Home_DF$SqFootage)) +

                scale_fill_discrete("Sq Footage") +

                scale_y_continuous("Counts") +
                scale_x_discrete("Year Built")

The as.character is used intentionally because it seemed like the only way to get the year label to show up directly below the data column on the histogram.

Now, is there a command within ggplot2 to reduce the number of years that appears and still have the year label appear directly below the data column?

Thanks again for any insights.

Home_Year_Built<-sample(1989:2008, size=sample_size, rep=T)
Home_Year_Sold<-sample(1989:2008, size=sample_size, rep=T)

# Now convert to semantic types
Home_SqFootage <- factor(Home_SqFootage)
Home_Year_Sold <- as.Date(as.character(Home_Year_Sold), "%Y")
Home_Year_Built <- as.Date(as.character(Home_Year_Built), "%Y")
# Note that this creates Date types for these columns, close to the
middle of the year

# Add to data frame
Home_DF<-data.frame(SqFootage=Home_SqFootage,
YearBuilt=Home_Year_Built, YearSold=Home_Year_Sold)

# Now plot
qplot(YearBuilt, data = Home_DF, binwidth = 365, fill = SqFootage)
# Don't want to do fill for binwidth=1, seems to take forever, seems
that binwidth for Date scales is in Days.

Seems like you'd want to convert SqFootage into some ranges, e.g.
Large, Small

Home_DF$SqFootage_Label <- recode(Home_SqFootage, "1200:2400='Small';
2401:3600='Large'", as.factor.result=T,levels=c("Large","Small"))
qplot(YearBuilt, data = Home_DF, binwidth = 365, fill = SqFootage_Label)

graph, if you let us know that we can help more.

messages.subject: Re: A way to only show every other label on scale_x_discrete?
messages.subject_clean: A way to only show every other label on scale_x_discrete?
messages.body_plain:
I would be very interested in knowing how to adjust the angle of the year or if that is even possible when using the as.character, which seems to be mandatory in order to get the year marker to line up directly below the data column.

Until then here is the work around (hack) I came up with to skip every other year:

sample_size<-200

Home_SqFootage<-sample(1200:3600, size=sample_size, rep=T)
Home_Year_Built<-sample(1989:2008, size=sample_size, rep=T)
Home_Year_Sold<-sample(1989:2008, size=sample_size, rep=T)
Home_DF<-data.frame(SqFootage=Home_SqFootage, YearBuilt=as.character(Home_Year_Built), YearSold=as.character(Home_Year_Sold))

label_length<-length(unique(Home_DF$YearBuilt))
all_labels<-sort(unique(Home_DF$YearBuilt))
new_label<-NULL
for(ii in 1:label_length)
{
        if(ii%%2 == 0)
        {
                new_label_tmp<-as.character(all_labels[ii])
        } else {
                new_label_tmp<-c("")
        }

        new_label<-c(new_label, new_label_tmp)
}

qplot(YearBuilt, data = Home_DF, binwidth = 1, fill = factor(Home_DF$SqFootage)) +
                     scale_fill_discrete("Sq Footage") +
                     scale_y_continuous("Counts") +

                     scale_x_discrete("Year Built", labels=new_label)

messages.subject: Combining text and graphical output ... slightly off-topic
messages.subject_clean: Combining text and graphical output ... slightly off-topic
messages.body_plain:
Slightly off topics, but relevant to making reliable graphics...

I'd like to produce a file that has both graphics and textual elements.

On page 1, for example, I'd like to have some textual information on
distributions - so that the graph - here Page 2 - is not disassociated
from the meta-data.

Clearly I can do that in Sweave, but I was trying not to involve another
step.  Ideally I'd have a graphics driver that would also generate
text... However, the pdf driver in particular, won't take text - even
though the PDF format clearly will hold both text and graphics.

Murrell and Jornik (http://www.ci.tuwien.ac.at/Conferences/DSC-2003/)
write "Text-based output is only possible for certain graphics
devices,... " but they do not mention which graphics devices would
support both.C

Suggestions welcome.

messages.subject_clean: Combining text and graphical output ... slightly off-topic
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I would still recommend the slight burden of Sweave, or alternatives such as:

- the brew package

- the ascii package

- odfSweave

- ... (there are probably others)

If you text (possibly with tables) is *very simple* though, you might
have some luck with custom grid functions. As an example,

library(RGraphics) # support of the "R graphics" book, on CRAN
library(gridextra) #  experimental package, http://code.google.com/p/gridextra/

g1 <- tableGrob(head(iris))

string <- "
This famous (Fisher's or Anderson's) iris data set gives the
measurements in centimeters of the variables sepal length and width
and petal length and width, respectively, for 50 flowers from each of
3 species of iris. The species are Iris setosa, versicolor, and
virginica.
"

g2 <- splitTextGrob(string)
#"Sepal.Length" "Sepal.Width"  "Petal.Length" "Petal.Width"  "Species"
g3 <- qplot(Sepal.Length,  Petal.Length, data=iris, colour=Species)

arrange2(g1, g2, g3, ncol=1, main="The iris data")

The output is attached.

HTH,

baptiste
